title: Finite coalgebra duality and its scalar-extension comparison
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $D$ a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space with linear maps $\Delta:D\to D\otimes_kD$ and $\epsilon:D\to k$ satisfying coassociativity and both counit identities. Use tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Put $A=\operatorname{Hom}_k(D,k)$ with convolution $(fg)(x)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta x)$ and unit $\epsilon$ (the tensor of two functionals is followed by multiplication in $k$). Then $A$ is a finite-dimensional associative unital $k$-algebra, not assumed commutative. Evaluation $D\to\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,k)$ is a linear isomorphism, and it restricts to a bijection between elements $x\in D$ satisfying $\Delta x=x\otimes x$, $\epsilon(x)=1$, and unital $k$-algebra homomorphisms $A\to k$. For every field extension $F/k$ [def-pc-field-extension], equip $D_F=F\otimes_kD$ with the scalar-extended coalgebra structure. The map $\theta_F:F\otimes_kA\to\operatorname{Hom}_F(D_F,F)$ defined by $\theta_F(a\otimes f)(b\otimes x)=abf(x)$ is an isomorphism of unital $F$-algebras, where the target has convolution multiplication. Zero-dimensional $D$ is allowed.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free], $D$ has a basis. It is finite: finitely many generators of $D$ have coordinates supported in a finite union $J$, so every basis vector belongs to the span of $J$ and hence has its index in $J$. Thus $D$ is finite free, and [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-projective] makes it projective. Apply [lem-sf-finite-projective-dual]: $A=D^*$ is finite-dimensional and the actual evaluation $e:D\to A^*$, $e(x)(f)=f(x)$, is a linear isomorphism. Apply [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra] with $(R,C,B)=(k,D,k)$ to obtain exactly the multiplication and unit of the statement. No cocommutativity is used.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 (finite coalgebra/algebra duality), and equation (77), printed p.237; the finite-dual scalar comparison and group-like character interpretation used in Theorem 12.18(c)⇒(d), printed p.238.

proof.text: If $\Delta x=x\otimes x$ and $\epsilon(x)=1$, then $e(x)(fg)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta x)=f(x)g(x)$ and $e(x)(\epsilon)=1$. Evaluation is $k$-linear, and the scalar map $c\mapsto c\epsilon$ is sent to $c\epsilon(x)=c$. Thus $e(x)$ is a unital $k$-algebra map. This verifies multiplicativity and scalar compatibility directly, without assuming that $A$ is commutative.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 (finite coalgebra/algebra duality), and equation (77), printed p.237; the finite-dual scalar comparison and group-like character interpretation used in Theorem 12.18(c)⇒(d), printed p.238.

proof.text: Conversely, let $\chi:A\to k$ be a unital $k$-algebra map. Its underlying linear functional has a unique preimage $x$ under the evaluation isomorphism of Step 1. Then $\epsilon(x)=\chi(1_A)=1$, and for all $f,g\in A$, $(f\otimes g)(\Delta x-x\otimes x)=\chi(fg)-\chi(f)\chi(g)=0$. By [lem-sfb-finite-free-tensor-dual] with $M=N=D$, every functional on $D\otimes_kD$ is a linear combination of these product functionals: the dual-tensor map is surjective and pure tensors span its source by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Therefore every functional vanishes on $z=\Delta x-x\otimes x$. If $z\ne0$, [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-dual-separates] applied to the vector space $D\otimes_kD$ gives a functional nonzero on $z$, a contradiction. Thus $x$ is group-like. Uniqueness in Step 1 proves the claimed bijection.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 (finite coalgebra/algebra duality), and equation (77), printed p.237; the finite-dual scalar comparison and group-like character interpretation used in Theorem 12.18(c)⇒(d), printed p.238.

proof.text: Apply the dual-scalar comparison in [lem-trf-projective-exterior-scalar-comparisons] with its $(A,B,V)$ equal to $(k,F,D)$. Step 1 supplies a finite-free presentation, hence the required finite-free retract (identity maps suffice). Its dual clause is exactly the $F$-linear isomorphism $\theta_F$ with $\theta_F(a\otimes f)(b\otimes x)=abf(x)$. For clarity the scalar-extended coalgebra maps are $\epsilon_F(b\otimes x)=b\epsilon(x)$ and $\Delta_F(b\otimes x)=\sum_i(b\otimes u_i)\otimes_F(1\otimes v_i)$ whenever $\Delta x=\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i$. These formulas respect tensor balancing. Evaluating the two coassociative composites on $b\otimes x$ gives $b$ times the scalar extension of the two composites for $x$; likewise each counit composite gives $b\otimes x$. The tensor generation statement [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] proves these identities everywhere. Consequently [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra] also supplies the convolution algebra on $D_F^*$.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 (finite coalgebra/algebra duality), and equation (77), printed p.237; the finite-dual scalar comparison and group-like character interpretation used in Theorem 12.18(c)⇒(d), printed p.238.

proof.text: For $a,c,b\in F$, $f,g\in A$ and $x\in D$, write $\Delta x=\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i$. Then $\theta_F((a\otimes f)(c\otimes g))(b\otimes x)=acb\sum_i f(u_i)g(v_i)$. Using the displayed formula for $\Delta_F$, the convolution product of $\theta_F(a\otimes f)$ and $\theta_F(c\otimes g)$ at $b\otimes x$ is $\sum_i abf(u_i)\,c g(v_i)$, the same quantity. The commutation used here is in $F$, not in $A$. Bilinearity and generation by pure tensors [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] extend equality to arbitrary inputs and arbitrary vectors of $D_F$. Finally $\theta_F(1\otimes\epsilon)(b\otimes x)=b\epsilon(x)=\epsilon_F(b\otimes x)$; $F$-linearity gives the scalar-map compatibility. Thus the linear isomorphism of Step 4 is the required unital $F$-algebra isomorphism.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 (finite coalgebra/algebra duality), and equation (77), printed p.237; the finite-dual scalar comparison and group-like character interpretation used in Theorem 12.18(c)⇒(d), printed p.238.

proof.text: When $D=0$, $A=0$ and both bidual and base-change maps are the unique isomorphisms between zero vector spaces. The convolution algebra is the zero algebra, allowed as a unital $k$-algebra. No $x$ satisfies $\epsilon(x)=1$, and there is no unital algebra homomorphism $0\to k$ since $0=1$ in its source but $0\ne1$ in $k$. Both sets in the bijection are therefore empty. All previous arguments also permit the empty basis.
